\chapter{Weather}
\label{ch:ge-weather}
\hlchaptermodality{21}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can talk about the weather in German — das Wetter, es ist heiß, es ist kalt, es regnet.}

Say das Wetter as English weather's own cousin, build hot and cold with sein rather than a Romance 'make', and say es regnet on the same root as English rain. The chapter's only lesson, so the payoff covers everything it introduces.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[das Wetter, es regnet]{das Wetter, es regnet — German's own native words, English's own cousins}

\label{lesson:GE-C21-das-wetter}



\begin{quote}
Every Romance language you've met so far shares the exact same Latin word for \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{} (\emph{tempus}). German breaks completely from that family — with a word that's actually a much closer cousin of English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words: das Wetter and weather}
\textbf{das Wetter} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{weather}\textquotedblright{} — from Proto-Germanic \emph{\textbf{wedrą}} — the \textbf{exact same word} as English \textbf{weather} itself (both descend from the same Germanic ancestor, not one borrowed from the other). Unlike Spanish's \emph{tiempo}, French's \emph{temps}, or Latin's own \emph{tempus}-family, German's weather word has \textbf{no connection to Latin at all} — it's a native Germanic inheritance, cousin to English rather than to Romance.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Es ist heiß / Es ist kalt}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Es ist heiß.} — \textquotedblleft{}It's hot.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}it \textbf{is} hot.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Es ist kalt.} — \textquotedblleft{}It's cold.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}it \textbf{is} cold.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

German uses \textbf{sein} (\textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}) here — matching the same \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{be}\textquotedblright{} pattern you already met in German's own AGE lesson (\emph{ich bin zwanzig}), not the Romance \textquotedblleft{}make\textquotedblright{} periphrasis (\emph{hacer}/\emph{faire}).
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Es regnet.} — \textquotedblleft{}It's raining.\textquotedblright{} — from \textbf{regnen} $\leftarrow$ Proto-Germanic \emph{\textbf{regnōną}} — the \textbf{same root} as English \textbf{rain}. Just like \emph{Wetter}/ \textquotedblleft{}weather,\textquotedblright{} this is a genuine Germanic cousin-pair, not a shared Latin borrowing the way Spanish's \emph{llueve} and French's \emph{pleut} are.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Wetter\textquotedblright{} — weather, the same word as English \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Es ist heiß. Es ist kalt.\textquotedblright{} — it's hot/cold
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Es regnet\textquotedblright{} — it's raining, same root as English \textquotedblleft{}rain\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \textbf{Wetter} come from Latin, like the Romance languages' weather words? (\textbf{No} — it's native Germanic, the same word as English \textquotedblleft{}weather.\textquotedblright{}) What verb does German use for \textquotedblleft{}it's hot/cold\textquotedblright{} — \emph{sein} (\textquotedblleft{}be\textquotedblright{}) or a \emph{hacer}-style \textquotedblleft{}make\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Sein}}, \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} — matching German's own AGE pattern.) What English word is \textbf{regnet} related to? (\textbf{Rain} — same Proto-Germanic root, \emph{regnōną}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
